overview.text: *Portugalophis lignites* is an extinct reptile from the Late Jurassic of Portugal, known only from pieces of its jaws. It was described in 2015 as one of the oldest known snakes, but a 2025 study of its group, the parviraptorids, left open whether they were snakes at all.

fossils.text: Two upper jaw bones (maxillae) and one lower jaw bone (dentary), from coal beds (lignites) in Portugal, which gave the species its name.

fossils.label: Find site
fossils.text: The Guimarota coal mine near Leiria.

geology.text: Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian), about 155 million years ago.

size.text: Not known: jaw fragments alone do not give a reliable body length.

uncertainty.text: When it was described, it was placed among the earliest snakes. Parviraptorids had been known only from very incomplete remains; a much more complete skeleton from the Isle of Skye, described in 2025, showed a mix of snake-like jaws and teeth with a lizard-like body. Its authors placed parviraptorids in their own family and left open whether they are early relatives of snakes or more primitive squamates that evolved snake-like jaws independently.

caldwell.title: The oldest known snakes from the Middle Jurassic-Lower Cretaceous provide insights on snake evolution
